{{Elections in Georgia (U.S. state) sidebar}}
The '''2026 Georgia gubernatorial election''' will take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Georgia]]. Incumbent [[Georgia Republican Party|Republican]] governor [[Brian Kemp]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. 

[[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026, with a primary runoff held on June 16. Businessman [[Rick Jackson (businessman)|Rick Jackson]] and incumbent Lieutenant Governor [[Burt Jones]] received the most votes in the first round of the Republican primary, but failed to reach the 50% threshold, causing a runoff which Jackson won. Jackson's campaign was predominantly self-funded, managing to overcome an endorsement for Jones from President [[Donald Trump]] and Kemp. Former [[Mayor of Atlanta|Atlanta Mayor]] [[Keisha Lance Bottoms]] won the Democratic nomination without a runoff against six other candidates.

The 2026 gubernatorial primary was the first time that Democratic turnout exceeded that of Republicans since [[2006 Georgia gubernatorial election|2006]].

If Lance Bottoms is elected, she would be the first female and first African-American governor of Georgia and could be the first female African-American governor in United States history. If Jackson is elected, he would be the oldest elected governor at the age of 72 surpassing [[Lamartine Griffin Hardman]].

== Background ==
Georgia is considered a [[swing state]] at the federal level, but the state has maintained a Republican lean at the state level, with Republicans holding all statewide executive offices in the [[2022 Georgia elections|2022 midterms]], where incumbent governor Brian Kemp was [[2022 Georgia gubernatorial election|re-elected]] in a rematch against [[Democratic Party of Georgia|Democrat]] [[Stacey Abrams]] by a 7.5 percent margin.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bluestein |first=Greg |title=Abrams says she will 'likely run again.' That doesn't excite some Democrats |language=English |work=[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]] |url=https://www.ajc.com/politics/abrams-says-she-will-likely-run-again-that-doesnt-excite-some-democrats/23WS3YRCB5E5FEVI5DPK6PU6LA/ |access-date=2023-05-13 |issn=1539-7459 |date=March 16, 2023}}</ref> Republicans also control both the [[Georgia State Senate|state senate]] and [[Georgia House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], together with Kemp's governorship establishing a [[government trifecta]], alongside an all but one Republican pick on the [[Supreme Court of Georgia (U.S. state)|state's supreme court]]. A year prior to the 2026 elections, the [[2025 Georgia Public Service Commission special election]] resulted in two Democrats being elected to the Commission, both by landslide victories, and marking the first time that Democrats won any seats on the PSC since the [[2000 Georgia state elections|2000 elections]] or any state-wide non-federal offices since the [[2006 Georgia state elections|2006 elections]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vakil |first=Caroline |date=November 4, 2025 |title=Democrats win key Georgia special elections seen as midterm bellwethers |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/5589670-gop-incumbents-lose-seats/ |access-date=November 12, 2025 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Emily |date=2025-11-06 |title=What Georgia Democrats' PSC wins could mean for power bills and the midterm elections |url=https://www.wabe.org/what-democrats-psc-wins-could-mean-for-power-bills-and-the-midterm-elections/ |access-date=2025-11-12 |website=WABE |language=en-US}}</ref> Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Georgia since [[1998 Georgia gubernatorial election|1998]].

== Republican primary ==

=== Candidates ===
With Kemp term-limited, speculation mounted about Lieutenant Governor [[Burt Jones]], Secretary of State [[Brad Raffensperger]], and Attorney General [[Chris Carr (politician)|Chris Carr]]. Carr and Raffensperger sought to associate themselves with Kemp, drawing on his relative popularity.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Timotija |first1=Filip |title=Georgia attorney general launches bid in 2026 governor’s race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5003295-georgia-chris-carr-governor-race/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |date=November 21, 2024}}</ref> Jones sought to ally himself with Trump, who endorsed him in August 2025. 

Rick Jackson, a healthcare CEO, announced his campaign in February 2026. Previously unknown in the political realm, Jackson quickly consolidated support from right-wing primary voters, in part due to his significant personal financial resources. Jackson spent more than $83 million in personal funds during the primary. Jackson's campaign emphasized his success as a self-made billionaire, highlighting his impoverished childhood. Jackson also sought to tie himself to Trump, claiming he would be "Trump's favorite governor" and "just like Trump, but with a Southern tone."<ref name="Trumps favorite governor">{{cite news |title=Burt Jones was the inevitable Republican nominee for Georgia governor. Then Rick Jackson showed up |url=https://apnews.com/article/rick-jackson-georgia-governor-burt-jones-trump-4c1789c599857e220180068e26de9199 |access-date=October 7, 2026 |agency=Associated Press |date=March 14, 2026}}</ref> An aggressive television ad campaign allowed Jackson to take a small polling lead by spring 2026. Jackson's self-funding represented the largest amount any candidate had ever spent in a primary race for Georgia governor.<ref name="Trumps favorite governor"></ref>

Jones's campaign focused primarily on rural connections, Trump, and support from Republican allies in the General Assembly. Jones accused Jackson of "made his fortune recruiting for [[Planned Parenthood]]" and funding [[Transgender surgery]] for minors.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bynum |first1=Zachary |title=Georgia GOP governor candidates Rick Jackson and Burt Jones clash over defamation lawsuit as the race heats up |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/atlanta/news/georgia-gop-governors-race-turns-messy-as-burt-jones-and-rick-jackson-clash-over-money-smears-and-campaign-tactics/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |agency=CBS News |date=March 10, 2026}}</ref> Jackson denied these accusations and filed for [[defamation]] against Jones, a lawsuit he later dropped.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rick Jackson drops lawsuits against Burt Jones as he seeks rival’s endorsement |url=https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/09/gop-candidate-for-governor-rick-jackson-drops-lawsuits-against-burt-jones/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |agency=Atlanta Journal-Constitution |date=September 22, 2026}}</ref>

Jones won a plurality of the vote at 38.4%, winning most rural counties. Jackson came second at 32.5%, drawing strong support from the north Atlanta suburbs. Raffensperger came in third and won [[DeKalb County, Georgia|DeKalb County]]. The lack of a majority meant that a runoff was held on June 16.

Jackson won the runoff by a 5-point margin, despite Kemp endorsing Jones two days before the vote. With the Democratic primary already over, focus shifted to the candidates' ability to counter Keisha Lance Bottoms. Jackson had consistently attacked Bottoms's record as mayor since he launched his campaign.

In the previous two occasions ([[2018 Georgia gubernatorial election|2018]] and [[2010 Georgia gubernatorial election|2010]]) where the Republican primary did not feature an incumbent governor, the plurality-winner in the primary went on to lose the primary runoff. This trend repeated itself in 2026.
